title: Xalwo Muus
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Over-ripe bananas mashed into a pan and cooked down for three quarters of an hour with sugar, butter and cardamom until they turn dark and sticky — the Bravanese halwa, made from fruit too far gone to eat.
longDesc: Known in Brava as halwa ya mazu, this is a thrift dish that became a delicacy. Twelve bananas nobody would eat raw go into a dry pan and reduce for half an hour before any sugar is added, by which point they have gone from pale mash to something dark and jam-like. Traditionally it was not portioned at all — it set as one large piece in a dish and everyone tore off what they wanted.
ingredients: // To shape and coat, if you are not serving it from the dish
A handful of pecans or other nuts, for stuffing
Shredded desiccated coconut, sesame seeds, crushed nuts or sweetened cocoa powder, for rolling
steps: Peel the bananas into a non-stick pan and mash them roughly.
Cook over medium heat for 30 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes. The mash will darken and thicken considerably.
Add the sugar and the melted butter.
Cook for a further 10 minutes, stirring continuously now — with the sugar in, it will catch if you leave it.
Add the cardamom and cook for 2 minutes more.
Either spoon it into a dish and serve it as one piece, or let it cool enough to handle and roll it into balls.
If shaping, press a nut into the centre of each ball, then roll them in coconut, sesame, crushed nuts or cocoa powder.
chefTips: The bananas must be genuinely over-ripe — black-skinned, the ones you would otherwise throw out. Firm bananas will not reduce to the right texture and you will end up adding sugar to compensate.
Thirty minutes before the sugar goes in is not negotiable. That is where the water cooks off and the flavour concentrates.
Once the sugar is in, stir constantly. Sugar plus a hot dry pan means it will scorch the moment your back is turned.
The balls-and-coating presentation is a modern refinement. Traditionally it was one large piece in a dish that people broke into, and that is still the better way to eat it.
commonMistakes: Adding the sugar at the start, which stops the bananas reducing properly and gives a wet, oversweet halwa.
Cooking it on high heat to save time — it burns on the base long before it thickens.
Using bananas that are merely ripe, which gives a pale, bland result.
Trying to shape it while still hot. It needs to cool enough to hold.
storage: Covered, at room temperature up to 5 days; refrigerated up to 2 weeks.
reheating: Serve at room temperature. A few seconds of warmth loosens it if it has set very firm.
healthBenefits: Bananas contribute potassium, vitamin B6 and fibre.
The sweetness comes largely from the fruit — half a cup of sugar across twelve bananas.
A use for fruit that would otherwise be wasted.
culturalNote: Brava's kitchens dried bananas in the sun as well — that product was called mazalfoorno — and halwa ya mazu is the cooked-down version of the same instinct: nothing in a coastal household with a banana tree went to waste. It is eaten with the unsweetened Somali coffee that cuts through it.
